commodityOwnIntro_metal: Most people own {{name}} through a fund or a mining company, not bars or coins. Today's moves:
commodityOwnIntro_oil: Nobody buys barrels. People own oil through a fund or an oil company. Today's moves:
commodityOwnNote_metal: Funds that hold the metal follow spot closely, minus a small yearly fee. Miners usually move more than the metal, in both directions.
commodityOwnNote_oil: Oil funds hold futures contracts, not barrels, so over months they can drift away from spot as they roll from one contract to the next. Oil companies also earn from refining, so they move less than oil.

commodityAbout_xau: The live price of one troy ounce of gold in US dollars. Traders call this the spot price: what gold costs for delivery right now.
commodityAbout_xag: The live price of one troy ounce of silver in US dollars. Traders call this the spot price: what silver costs for delivery right now.
commodityAbout_xpt: The live price of one troy ounce of platinum in US dollars. Traders call this the spot price: what platinum costs for delivery right now.
commodityAbout_xpd: The live price of one troy ounce of palladium in US dollars. Traders call this the spot price: what palladium costs for delivery right now.
commodityAbout_wti: The live price of one barrel of West Texas Intermediate crude in US dollars, the main benchmark for US oil. Traders call this the spot price.
commodityAbout_xbr: The live price of one barrel of Brent crude in US dollars. Brent comes from the North Sea and is the benchmark for most of the world's oil. Traders call this the spot price.
commodityDriver_gold_1: Interest rates. Gold pays no interest, so it tends to fall when rates after inflation rise, and gain when they drop.
commodityDriver_gold_2: The US dollar. Gold is priced in dollars, so a weaker dollar usually means a higher gold price.
commodityDriver_gold_3: Central banks. Central banks hold gold in their reserves, and their buying or selling shifts demand.
commodityDriver_gold_4: Fear. In wars, crises and market crashes, investors often buy gold as a safe place to keep money.
commodityDriver_silver_1: Industry. More than half of all silver goes into electronics, solar panels and other industrial uses, so it follows the economy more than gold does.
commodityDriver_silver_2: Gold's drivers. Interest rates, the dollar and fear move silver too, usually in the same direction as gold.
commodityDriver_silver_3: Bigger swings. The silver market is much smaller than gold's, so its price tends to move further on the same news.
commodityDriver_pgm_1: Cars. A large share goes into catalytic converters that clean car exhaust, so car sales and the shift to electric cars matter.
commodityDriver_pgm_2: Supply. Most of it is mined in a few places, mainly South Africa and Russia, so mine problems or sanctions can move the price fast.
commodityDriver_pgm_3: A small market. Far less is traded than gold or silver, so the price can jump on modest news.
commodityDriver_oil_1: OPEC+. The group of oil producers led by Saudi Arabia and Russia decides how much to pump, and its decisions can move oil within hours.
commodityDriver_oil_2: The economy. Demand rises and falls with travel, shipping and factories, so signs of a slowdown usually push oil lower.
commodityDriver_oil_3: US stockpiles. The US government reports how much oil is in storage every Wednesday. A bigger build than expected usually pushes the price down.
commodityDriver_oil_4: Conflict. Wars and attacks near oil fields or shipping routes raise the risk of lost supply.
commodityDiffTitle: Spot, funds and companies: what is the difference?
commodityDiff_metal: The spot price is what the metal itself costs today. A fund like GLD owns the metal for you, so its price follows spot but is a different number: compare percentage moves, not prices. A mining company adds a business on top, with its own costs and debt, so its shares can rise or fall more than the metal.
commodityDiff_oil: The spot price is what a barrel costs for delivery today. A fund like USO holds futures, contracts to buy oil later, and has to keep replacing them, which can cost money over time. An oil company earns from pumping and refining, so its shares follow oil only partly.
